ledger.sentence: The NHS invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 in England, and the first invitation arrives a few months before the 25th birthday.
People registered as female with a GP are invited automatically.
Trans men and non-binary people who are registered differently may need to ask through their GP or a sexual health or transgender clinic.
Routine screening is every five years.
Since 1 July 2025, people aged 25 to 49 with a negative HPV test have moved from a three-year to a five-year interval.
Invitations usually stop at 65, and a person is invited again only if a recent test was abnormal.
Most screening takes place at a GP surgery, and a person can ask for a female nurse or doctor.
The person undresses from the waist down behind a screen and lies back on a bed.
The clinician gently puts a smooth, tube-shaped tool called a speculum into the vagina, and a soft brush collects a sample of cells from the cervix.
The test itself takes under five minutes, and the whole appointment is about ten minutes.
People can ask for a smaller speculum, ask to stop at any time, or ask to insert the speculum themselves.
Light spotting for a few hours afterwards is normal.
Current NHS practice tests the sample for high-risk HPV first.
The NHS England guide says high-risk HPV can cause abnormal cell changes that may lead to cervical cancer.
If HPV is found, the laboratory then looks more closely at the cells for changes.
If no HPV is found, the NHS says the risk of cervical cancer is very low, and routine screening is usually five years later.
If HPV is found but the cells are normal, the person is usually retested in about 12 months.
If HPV continues after two years, an invitation for a colposcopy follows.
If HPV is found with abnormal cells, the person is referred for a colposcopy.
An unclear sample means a repeat test, which does not mean anything is wrong.
Results usually arrive by letter, and one source gives two weeks, sometimes longer.
ledger.note: Summary: results timing from one source.

ledger.sentence: A colposcopy is a closer look at the cervix, done in a hospital or clinic.
The NHS says most people who have one do not have cervical cancer.
Biopsy results grade the cell changes: low-grade changes usually need no immediate treatment, and high-grade changes are offered treatment to remove the cells.
Unusual vaginal bleeding, such as between periods or after sex, needs a GP appointment, because screening is not meant for symptoms.
The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening.
The sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus that can lead to cell changes.
A negative HPV result means the risk of cervical cancer is very low, and the next routine test is usually in five years.
Most people who have a colposcopy do not have cervical cancer.
Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment and what each result means.
